newsitem.title: USA: Clinton widens lead to 15 percent - Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton widens lead to 15 percent - Reuters poll.

text.p: President Bill Clinton stretched his lead over Republican Bob Dole to 15.1 percentage points in a Reuters poll released on Tuesday, and the pollster said a Clinton "landslide" victory was becoming a possibility.

Clinton got 47.4 percent support to Dole's 32.3 percent in the poll, conducted by John Zogby Group International. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot had 5.3 percent; 2.5 percent picked "other" and 12.4 percent were undecided.
The poll tracks about 900 likely voters over a three-day period. The latest result, with a 3.3 percentage point margin of error, reflects polling on Saturday through Monday.

Pollster John Zogby said this was the eighth straight day that Clinton's lead had increased, and noted that Dole's numbers remained in the low 30s, even though he got a boost from the first presidential debate on October 6.
For the first time, a majority of likely voters -- 50.6 percent -- answered "yes" to the question, "Does President Clinton deserve to be re-elected?" A comparable question was not asked for Dole.
"This is not only a potential for a landslide, but into the zone where Clinton's coattails can usher in a Democratic Congress," Zogby said.
In the battle for Congress -- under Republican majority control since the 1994 election -- the poll showed an overall 5.8 percentage point lead for Democratic candidates.
Asked which party's candidate they would vote for in their congressional district, 38.3 percent said they would vote for a Democrat and 32.5 percent for a Republican.
Zogby said Democrats were now edging up as the preferred party to rule both the Senate -- by 41.2 percent to 39.3 percent -- and the House of Representatives, with 42 percent over 37.3 percent.

The poll showed Dole holding seven of 10 Republican votes and nearly six in 10 voters who feel the country is on the "wrong track". But his only lead in a key region is in the South, where his margin is barely outside the 3.3 percent margin of error at 41.3 percent to 38.7 percent over Clinton.

By contrast, Clinton leads "dramatically" in every other region, according to Zogby, among independent voters, among all age groups, among Roman Catholics, among moderates and among those who have lost a job in the past year and those who are working for less.
Zogby characterised the gender gap -- in which women favour Clinton more than men do -- as being "as big as the Grand Canyon."
